summary: Imperial Beach sits at the southwesternmost corner of the contiguous United States — literally the last beach town before the Mexican border — and that geographic oddity shapes everything about it. At just 4.4 square miles, it's tiny and flat, pinched between the Pacific Ocean to the west and the Tijuana River National Estuarine Research Reserve to the south, one of the last undeveloped coastal wetlands in Southern California, offering miles of trails through salt marsh and dune habitat minutes from the surf. The climate is absurdly mild, with average highs around 70°F year-round and nearly nine hours of daily sunshine, yet the median home price of $811,000 against a median household income of roughly $79,000 produces a price-to-income ratio above 10:1 — making ownership a stretch without substantial outside capital. Rents averaging $1,914 consume a meaningful share of that same income. This is overwhelmingly a bedroom community; Naval Air Station North Island and other military installations across the bay in Coronado are major employment anchors, and most workers commute north along the Silver Strand or I-5 into greater San Diego. The town's compact grid, pier, and small commercial strips along Palm Avenue give it a distinct, slightly scruffy beach-village identity rather than a polished resort feel — a place defined by the tension between an extraordinary natural setting and the economic pressure that setting inevitably attracts.
